title: Netflix's 'A Toxic Love Story' Exposes a U.S. Marshal's Scheme to Frame His Ex-Fiancée
excerpt: A new true crime documentary traces how Deputy U.S. Marshal Ian Diaz and his wife Angela Connell orchestrated a cyberstalking hoax that sent innocent Michelle Hadley to prison for 88 days.
body:
When Michelle Hadley broke off her engagement to Deputy U.S. Marshal Ian Diaz in August 2015, she thought she was finally free from a controlling relationship. Within months, she was behind bars — arrested for crimes she never committed, held on $1 million bail, and facing charges that carried decades in prison.

Netflix's A Toxic Love Story, which premiered on July 23, unspools what the Department of Justice would later call one of the most brazen framing schemes in recent memory. Using police body camera footage, court records, and first-person interviews — including Hadley speaking publicly for the first time — the documentary reveals how a federal law enforcement officer weaponized his badge and his new wife to destroy his ex.

The Setup

Hadley, now 39, met Diaz in the summer of 2013. He was a clean-cut U.S. Marshal who took her to Disneyland on their first date. They got engaged and bought a condo together in Anaheim, California. But behind the fairy-tale exterior, according to Hadley, Diaz installed surveillance cameras in their home and controlled her movements.

After Hadley left, Diaz married Angela Connell in February 2016 — just six months later — and moved her into the contested condo. Within weeks, the newlyweds told police they were being targeted by a mysterious online stalker calling themselves "Lilithistruth," who sent threatening emails with biblical overtones and images of decapitated fetuses. They pointed the finger squarely at Hadley.

The accusations escalated. Angela claimed someone had posted her photos on Craigslist "rape fantasy" ads to lure men to her home, and that she had been physically assaulted by a man in a black ski mask in their garage. The Anaheim Police Department arrested Hadley in July 2016.

The Unraveling

The case began to crack when Department of Justice Special Agent Jason Higley took a closer look. Because Diaz was a federal employee, the DOJ's Office of the Inspector General had jurisdiction. Higley noticed that in body camera footage, Diaz appeared to be coaching Angela during police interviews. He also found that Diaz had navigated directly to the specific Craigslist ad — something that would be nearly impossible unless he already knew exactly where to look.

The clincher: fragments of emails sent by "Lilithistruth" were found on Diaz's DOJ-issued laptop. The entire scheme — the threatening emails, the staged assaults, the Craigslist ads — had been orchestrated by the couple themselves.

"It turns your whole world upside down, and it really did feel like being buried alive because it just felt like I was so powerless. You don't have access to outside information. You're just so at the mercy of the system."

— Michelle Hadley, speaking to USA Today

A Pattern of Deception

The documentary also reveals Angela Connell's history of fraud. Her ex-boyfriend Jason Rayburn and former friend Mary Bukovskis describe how Connell fabricated a Stage 4 cervical cancer diagnosis, faked chemotherapy treatments using photos found online, and manufactured positive pregnancy tests with blue markers and ziplock bags. The twins she told Diaz she was carrying never existed.

On January 6, 2017, Angela was arrested and pleaded guilty to fraud, false imprisonment, and falsely reporting a crime. She was sentenced to five years in state prison. Diaz was arrested in May 2021 and convicted on all counts — conspiracy to commit cyberstalking, cyberstalking, perjury, and obstruction of a federal proceeding. He received 121 months in federal prison, where he remains. He was dismissed from the U.S. Marshals Service in 2023.

Life After Exoneration

Hadley was exonerated in January 2017, but the damage ran deep. She struggled to find work, eventually relocating across the country to New York City to restart her career in marketing. She successfully sued the Anaheim Police Department and was awarded significant damages in 2021.

"I never felt like I really had a chance to reclaim the narrative, and most importantly, to tell the story about the domestic abuse that I experienced in the relationship."

— Michelle Hadley

In a striking coincidence, Hadley gave birth to her daughter on the same day Ian Diaz was convicted in 2023. She now works in customer relationsship management and has spent over 15 years in the field.

The documentary, directed by Alexandra Lacey and produced by Emma Supple, arrives at a moment when questions about law enforcement accountability and the criminal justice system's capacity to recognize victims of institutional manipulation remain urgent. As Supple told Netflix: "Much of what happened took place behind closed doors. The reality was far more complex than the headlines had suggested."
